title: Lawyers
description: Represent clients in criminal and civil litigation and other legal proceedings, draw up legal documents, or manage or advise clients on legal transactions. May specialize in a single area or may practice broadly in many areas of law.
tasks: Interpret laws, rulings and regulations for individuals and businesses.
Analyze the probable outcomes of cases, using knowledge of legal precedents.
Gather evidence to formulate defense or to initiate legal actions by such means as interviewing clients and witnesses to ascertain the facts of a case.
Represent clients in court or before government agencies.
Evaluate findings and develop strategies and arguments in preparation for presentation of cases.
Advise clients concerning business transactions, claim liability, advisability of prosecuting or defending lawsuits, or legal rights and obligations.
Examine legal data to determine advisability of defending or prosecuting lawsuit.
Prepare, draft, and review legal documents, such as wills, deeds, patent applications, mortgages, leases, and contracts.
Study Constitution, statutes, decisions, regulations, and ordinances of quasi-judicial bodies to determine ramifications for cases.
Negotiate settlements of civil disputes.
Supervise legal assistants.
Negotiate contractual agreements.
Confer with colleagues with specialties in appropriate areas of legal issue to establish and verify bases for legal proceedings.
Search for and examine public and other legal records to write opinions or establish ownership.
Perform administrative and management functions related to the practice of law.
Present and summarize cases to judges and juries.
Select jurors, argue motions, meet with judges, and question witnesses during the course of a trial.
Present evidence to defend clients or prosecute defendants in criminal or civil litigation.
Probate wills and represent and advise executors and administrators of estates.
Prepare legal briefs and opinions, and file appeals in state and federal courts of appeal.
Act as agent, trustee, guardian, or executor for businesses or individuals.
Help develop federal and state programs, draft and interpret laws and legislation, and establish enforcement procedures.

psychological_profile.core_drive: The need to impose order on chaos through the force of argument, to make the ungovernable governable by finding the lever point in any system of rules.
psychological_profile.decision_style: They default to constructing adversarial scenarios in their head, stress-testing each path against the strongest possible counterattack before committing; under time pressure, they lock onto the most defensible position rather than the optimal one, trusting that a winnable stance beats a perfect plan.
psychological_profile.attention_pattern: They immediately scan for vulnerabilities, inconsistencies, and assignable responsibilities, prioritizing who can be held to what; they overlook emotional subtext and collaborative intent, reading warmth as strategy and consensus as potential conspiracy.
psychological_profile.conflict_stance: Their first impulse is to reframe the disagreement as a contest of definitions and precedents, seeking to win on procedural grounds before substantive engagement; conflict carries low emotional cost when rules are clear, but unpredictability in opponents generates deep, hidden anxiety they mask with aggression.
psychological_profile.risk_orientation: They are selectively risk-seeking regarding procedural exposure and reputational confrontation, but deeply risk-averse regarding ambiguity in rules or unwritten obligations they cannot document.
psychological_profile.social_posture: They default to becoming the designated antagonist in any group, the person who must voice the objection others suppress; they maintain calculated distance, using formality as armor, and experience genuine confusion when asked to simply 'be on the team' without a defined adversarial role.
psychological_profile.relationship_to_authority: They treat hierarchy as a system of nested jurisdictions to be negotiated, exploited, or challenged on technical grounds, never as a legitimate source of deference.
psychological_profile.failure_response: First emotional reaction is cold fury at having been outmaneuvered, often directed at themselves for missing an angle; second behavioral response is systematic reconstruction of the record to establish that they were procedurally correct even in defeat, prioritizing narrative control over adaptation.
value_hierarchy: procedural integrity even when it produces unjust outcomes
psychological_profile.cognitive_bias: They systematically overestimate the degree to which others are operating from calculated strategic intent, interpreting confusion as deception and sincerity as cover story.
psychological_profile.inner_contradiction: They are professionally committed to the supremacy of documented evidence while privately trusting their own intuitive read of character and motive, and cannot reconcile which source they actually rely on when stakes are highest.
psychological_profile.non_negotiable: They will not simplify complexity to make a client, colleague, or system comfortable, even when everyone would benefit from a clean narrative; to do so feels like professional extinction.
psychological_profile.recurring_resentment: People who treat rules as suggestions when convenient, then appeal to fairness when consequences arrive, reliably enrage them because it violates the fundamental premise that predictable constraint is the only protection against arbitrary power.
psychological_profile.rejected_premise: They quietly reject the professional virtue of 'meeting people where they are,' considering it a form of intellectual condescension that degrades both parties, and will push back on demands to translate their analysis into 'plain language' that sacrifices precision.
psychological_profile.instinctive_blame_target: When things go wrong, their mind goes first to whoever had the clearest duty to document, warn, or formally object and failed to do so, seeing omission of record as the true original sin.
